# Hello, deck

A code-first slide system: one MDX or TSX file per slide, ordered by `deck.config.ts`.

<Notes>
Welcome everyone. This deck exercises the engine: steps, notes and a TSX slide.
</Notes>

slides.title: How steps work
slides.source:
---
layout: default
title: How steps work
budget: 1m30s
---

## How steps work

<Step at={1}>
- Each slide has one integer step, starting at 0.
</Step>

<Step at={2}>
- `<Step at={n}>` reveals its content from step n on.
</Step>

<Step at={3}>
- Going back into a slide lands on its last step.
</Step>

<Notes>
Press the right arrow three times to reveal each point.

Mention that the step count comes from the steps that mount.
</Notes>

Decks as code: written by people or agents, signed off by a designer.

<Notes>
Good evening. This deck is its own demo: every slide you are about to see is a text file, and nothing in those files says what colour or size anything is.

By the end you will know whether you could write your next talk this way, or let an agent write the first draft.

Transition: first, who is talking.
</Notes>

slides.title: A slide is a file, the brand owns the pixels, a linter checks the result
slides.source:
---
layout: statement
title: A slide is a file, the brand owns the pixels, a linter checks the result
eyebrow: The claim
budget: 40s
---

A slide is a file. The brand owns every pixel. A linter tells the author, human or agent, what is wrong.

<Notes>
Three sentences, and the rest of the talk is evidence for them. [pause]

A slide is a file: you can diff it, review it, generate it. The brand owns every pixel: an author cannot pick a colour or a type size. And the linter renders the deck and measures it, so "it overflows" is a finding with a fix, not an opinion.

Transition: how does that compare with what you use today?
</Notes>

slides.title: Three ways to make a deck, measured alike
slides.source:
---
layout: comparison
title: Three ways to make a deck, measured alike
eyebrow: Where it sits
options:
  - name: Slide app
    summary: Boxes placed by hand
  - name: Generated HTML
    summary: One page per prompt
  - name: Deckster
    summary: Files, layouts, lint
    recommended: true
rows:
  - label: Stays on brand
    values: [By discipline, By luck, By construction]
    winner: 3
  - label: Text fits
    values: [You look, Nobody looks, Lint measures]
    winner: 3
  - label: Free placement
    values: [Drag anything, Edit markup, Layouts only]
    winner: 1
  - label: Reviewable diff
    values: [false, true, true]
  - label: PowerPoint file
    values: [true, false, true]
budget: 1m
---

<Footnote>A judgement, not a benchmark: what each approach guarantees without extra effort.</Footnote>

<Notes>
A slide app lets you put anything anywhere, and that is exactly why brand and fit depend on discipline. Generated HTML is fast and unchecked: it looks right until a title gets longer.

Deckster gives up free placement on purpose. Look at the third row: that one it loses. In exchange the brand holds by construction and the fit is measured.

Transition: four questions decide whether that trade works for you.
</Notes>

One file per slide, ordered by one config, styled by nobody.

<Notes>
Part one. If you remember one thing from it: the author writes the claim and the evidence, and nothing else.
</Notes>

```mdx title="slides/review-rounds.mdx" {1-5|9-11|7}
<LineChart data="rounds" x="month" highlight="2026" />

Say the claim, then point at June.
```

<Aside>

- Frontmatter picks a layout and states the claim

- Notes hold what the speaker says

</Aside>

<Notes>
This is a whole slide. [click] The frontmatter: which layout, the title as a sentence, and how long I plan to talk.

[click] The notes, which you are hearing now.

[click] And the body: one chart. No size, no position, no colour.

<Svg src="../assets/canvas.svg" title="The 1920 by 1080 slide canvas: brand margins, the shared title line, the content region and the chrome" steps={{ margins: 1, titleline: 2, region: 3, chrome: 4 }} recolor={{ "#e4572e": "accent", "#9aa1ae": "edge", "#ffffff": "bg", "#f4f5f8": "group", "#161920": "fg", "#555c6a": "label" }} draw />

<Notes>
The canvas is always 1920 by 1080. [click] The brand sets the margins. [click] Every title sits on the same line, so slides do not jump when you advance. [click] Under it is the region: the room a chart, a diagram or a table sizes itself to. [click] And the chrome, page number and logo, lives in the margins.

Transition: a layout is how a slide claims part of that canvas.
</Notes>

slides.title: A layout is a contract with four clauses
slides.source:
---
layout: cards
title: A layout is a contract with four clauses
eyebrow: Layouts
cards:
  - icon: list-check
    title: Typed fields
    text: Frontmatter is validated; a typo fails.
  - icon: layout-grid
    title: Named slots
    text: Each slot lists the content it accepts.
  - icon: scale
    title: A content budget
    text: Words and bullets, never pixels.
  - icon: columns-3
    title: Variants
    text: Tighter limits when a slide gets denser.
reveal: true
budget: 1m
---

The build and the linter enforce every clause, in every brand.

<Notes>
Four clauses. [click] Fields are typed, so `titel` with a typo is a build error. [click] Slots say what they take: this one a chart, that one three bullets. [click] The budget counts content, words and bullets, so a slide inside its budget in one brand is inside it in all of them. [click] And variants tighten the limits when you pick the dense version, four cards instead of three.

Transition: and none of those limits is a secret.
</Notes>

<Table

<Footnote>Read from the layout catalog in this repository; a layout's variants tighten these further.</Footnote>

<Notes>
These are real limits, straight from the catalog an agent reads before it writes. A content slide takes a ninety-character title. A split, where the title shares the width with a picture, takes forty-four.

An author who knows the limit before writing does not write a title that needs shrinking. An agent that knows it does not either.

Transition: and when the content outgrows a form, you change the form.
</Notes>

slides.title: A bullet list becomes cards in one edit
slides.source:
---
layout: code
title: A bullet list becomes cards in one edit
eyebrow: Changing form
budget: 1m
---

<CodeMove file="slides/lint-checks.mdx">

```mdx
---
layout: content
title: Lint checks twice
---

- Schema
- Rendered
```

```mdx
---
layout: cards
title: Lint checks twice
cards:
  - icon: braces
    title: Schema
  - icon: ruler
    title: Rendered
---
```

</CodeMove>

<Aside>

- The claim stays, the form changes
- Icons come from the brand's set
- An unknown icon fails the build

</Aside>

<Notes>
Here is a list that wants to be something better. [click] Same title, same two ideas, now as cards with icons. The tokens you just watched glide are the ones that survived the edit.

Nobody chose a grid, a gap or an icon size.

Transition: which raises the question of what a slide file is not allowed to say.
</Notes>

slides.title: What a slide file never contains
slides.source:
---
layout: default
title: What a slide file never contains
budget: 1m
---

## What a slide file never contains

<Step at={1}>
- A colour: surfaces and roles belong to the brand
</Step>

<Step at={2}>
- A type size: the layout picks the step and fits it
</Step>

<Step at={3}>
- A position: slots place content inside the margins
</Step>

<Step at={4}>
- A workaround: lint reports raw values as `off-brand`
</Step>

<Notes>
Four things you will not find in any file of this deck. [click] No colour. [click] No type size. [click] No position. [click] And if someone sneaks one in, the linter calls it off-brand and says which token to use.

This is the designer's half of the deal: the brand cannot be overridden from a slide.

Transition: so how much can you say with only layouts and components?
</Notes>

slides.title: A slide passes two checkpoints between the file and the screen
slides.source:
---
layout: diagram
title: A slide passes two checkpoints between the file and the screen
eyebrow: How a slide renders
budget: 1m30s
---

<Flow title="A slide file validated by the build, placed by its layout and drawn on the canvas">
  <Node id="file" kind="document" title="Slide file" subtitle="MDX or TSX" col={1} row={1} />
  <Node id="build" kind="function" title="Build" subtitle="Validates the file" col={2} row={1} />
  <Node id="layout" kind="service" title="Layout" subtitle="Fills its slots" col={3} row={1} />
  <Node id="canvas" kind="client" title="Canvas" subtitle="1920 × 1080" col={4} row={1} />
  <Node id="catalog" kind="database" title="Layout catalog" subtitle="Fields and budgets" col={2} row={2} />
  <Node id="brand" kind="document" title="brand.ts" subtitle="Tokens and type" col={3} row={2} />
  <Edge from="file" to="build" label="content" />
  <Edge from="catalog" to="build" label="contract" />
  <Edge from="build" to="layout" label="props" />
  <Edge from="brand" to="layout" label="tokens" />
  <Edge from="layout" to="canvas" label="DOM" />
  <Journey at={1} path="file build layout canvas" trail />
</Flow>

<Notes>
Follow the dot. [click] The file goes to the build, which checks it against the layout's contract: unknown field, wrong slot, title too long, and you get an error with the fix.

[click] The layout takes the validated content and fills its slots, reading every value from the brand.

[click] And the result lands on the canvas, scaled to whatever screen you have.

Two inputs the author never touches: the catalog and the brand.

Transition: those boxes are packages, and they stack.
</Notes>

slides.title: Five layers, and an author only ever edits the top one
slides.source:
---
layout: diagram
title: Five layers, and an author only ever edits the top one
eyebrow: Architecture
surface: inverse
budget: 1m
---

<Layers title="The framework in five layers, from a deck's content down to the tooling">
  <Layer title="Your deck" subtitle="Content" at={1}>
    <Item kind="document" title="Slides" />
    <Item kind="document" title="Config" />
    <Item kind="storage" title="Assets" />
  </Layer>
  <Layer title="Kit" subtitle="Layouts and components" at={2}>
    <Item kind="service" title="Layouts" />
    <Item kind="service" title="Charts" />
    <Item kind="service" title="Diagrams" />
    <Item kind="service" title="Media" />
  </Layer>
  <Layer title="Engine" subtitle="Renders a deck" at={3}>
    <Item kind="client" title="Canvas" />
    <Item kind="function" title="Steps" />
    <Item kind="gateway" title="Navigation" />
  </Layer>
  <Layer title="Brand" subtitle="Owns the look" at={4}>
    <Item kind="document" title="Tokens" />
    <Item kind="document" title="Type scale" />
    <Item kind="storage" title="Icon set" />
  </Layer>
  <Layer title="Tooling" subtitle="CLI and Vite plugin" at={5}>
    <Item kind="function" title="dev" />
    <Item kind="function" title="lint" />
    <Item kind="function" title="shot" />
    <Item kind="function" title="export" />
  </Layer>
</Layers>

<Notes>
Top to bottom. [click] Your deck: slides, a config, assets. That is all an author or an agent edits. [click] The kit: layouts and components. [click] The engine renders and navigates. [click] The brand owns the look. [click] And the tooling checks and ships it.

A designer works in layer four. Everyone else stays in layer one.

Transition: evidence is not only drawings. Some of it moves.
</Notes>

slides.title: Text over a photo stays readable
slides.source:
---
layout: image
title: Text over a photo stays readable
eyebrow: The image layout
focal: center 40%
budget: 30s
---

The layout puts a scrim behind each block of text, and lint measures contrast against the pixels underneath.

<Media>
  <Image src="../assets/westgate-street.jpg" alt="A residential street under a full summer canopy of mature maples" />
</Media>

<Caption>Westgate, July. Photo: Onthehilltop, CC0.</Caption>

<Notes>
A bright, busy photo is the classic way to lose a title. Here the layout sizes a scrim to the text, and the linter checks the contrast against the real pixels under each glyph, not against a guess.

I did not write a gradient. I wrote a title and pointed at a file.

Transition: last kind of evidence: something that runs.
</Notes>

A brand nobody can override, and a linter that renders before it judges.

slides.title: Rebranding a deck is a one-line diff
slides.source:
---
layout: code
title: Rebranding a deck is a one-line diff
eyebrow: Brands
surface: gradient
budget: 1m
---

```ts title="decks/showcase/deck.config.ts" diff
export default defineDeck({
  title: 'Slides an agent can write',
-  brand: 'default',
+  brand: 'nocturne',
  duration: '45m',
  slides: ['cover', 'speaker', 'the-claim'],
});
```

<Aside>

- Surfaces, type, icons and charts all follow
- `--brand nocturne` previews it with no edit
- Budgets count words, so the text still fits

</Aside>

<Notes>
This is the config of the deck you are watching. One line changes and every slide is in another brand: other fonts, other colours, another icon set, other chart palettes.

You do not even need the edit. Lint, shot and dev take a brand flag, so you can check a deck in a brand it was not written for. This deck passes in both.

Transition: at Halden that is not a party trick, it is the business.
</Notes>

slides.title: Lint renders every step in a real browser, then measures what it drew
slides.source:
---
layout: diagram
title: Lint renders every step in a real browser, then measures what it drew
eyebrow: How lint works
budget: 1m30s
---

<Flow title="deck lint serving the deck, rendering each step in Chromium, measuring it and reporting findings">
  <Node id="deck" kind="document" title="Deck" subtitle="Slides and config" col={1} row={1} />
  <Node id="server" kind="service" title="Dev server" subtitle="Static mode" col={2} row={1} />
  <Node id="chromium" kind="client" title="Chromium" subtitle="Every step" col={3} row={1} />
  <Node id="snapshot" kind="database" title="Snapshot" subtitle="Boxes, text, colours" col={3} row={2} />
  <Node id="rules" kind="function" title="42 rules" subtitle="Measure and compare" col={2} row={2} />
  <Node id="findings" kind="document" title="Findings" subtitle="File, rule, fix" col={1} row={2} />
  <Edge from="deck" to="server" label="serve" />
  <Edge from="server" to="chromium" label="render" />
  <Edge from="chromium" to="snapshot" label="measure" />
  <Edge from="snapshot" to="rules" label="check" />
  <Edge from="rules" to="findings" label="report" />
  <Packet path="deck server chromium" at={1} label="slide 7" />
  <State node="chromium" at={1} until={2} is="highlighted" />
  <Packet path="chromium snapshot rules" at={2} />
  <State node="rules" at={3} until={4} is="error" badge="Overflow" />
  <Packet path="rules findings" at={3} label="fix" />
  <State node="rules" at={4} is="success" />
  <State node="findings" at={4} is="success" badge="Clean" />
</Flow>

<Notes>
The linter does not read your source and guess. [click] It serves the deck and opens every step of every slide in Chromium. [click] It measures what was drawn: every box, every line of text, the colours under the glyphs. [click] Forty-two rules run over that snapshot. Here one fires: overflow. The finding carries the file, the rule and the fix. [click] You fix it, run again, clean.

That is why the same check works for a person and for an agent: the finding is text with an instruction in it.

Transition: here is what that looked like for this deck.
</Notes>

slides.title: Lint names the file, the rule and the fix
slides.source:
---
layout: code
title: Lint names the file, the rule and the fix
eyebrow: Real output, this deck
surface: inverse
budget: 1m15s

<Terminal title="~/deckster" at={1}>
  <Cmd>pnpm deck lint showcase</Cmd>
  <Out tone="error">error  content-budget (bullets-to-cards)</Out>
  <Out>The body slot holds 13 lines; its layout allows 11.</Out>
  <Out tone="muted">Fix: Cut it to the essentials, split the slide, …</Out>
  <Out tone="error">showcase: 1 error, 0 warnings in 12 slides</Out>
  <Cmd>pnpm deck lint showcase</Cmd>
  <Out tone="success">showcase: no problems in 12 slides</Out>
  <Cmd>pnpm deck lint showcase --brand nocturne</Cmd>
  <Out tone="success">showcase: no problems in 22 slides</Out>
</Terminal>

<Aside>

<Lottie src="../assets/check.json" alt="A check mark drawing itself inside a ring" size="md" role="fg" />

- A finding from this deck's first draft
- Exit code 1 until it is fixed

</Aside>

<Notes>
This is copied from my terminal while I wrote this deck. [click] First run, twelve slides in: the code slide you saw earlier had thirteen lines in a layout that allows eleven. Rule, slide, and what to do about it.

[click] I cut a card. Clean.

[click] Ten slides later, the same deck in the other brand. Also clean.

Notice what is not on screen: no stack trace, no selector soup. A sentence about the slide, and a sentence about what to do.

If asked: the output is shortened to fit; the full fix line lists four options.

Transition: what do first drafts usually get wrong?
</Notes>

slides.title: A review comment resolves to a file and a line, or says that it cannot
slides.source:

layout: diagram
title: A review comment resolves to a file and a line, or says that it cannot
eyebrow: Review comments
budget: 1m15s

<Tree title="How a review comment finds its line again after the slide was edited">
  <Node id="reviewer" kind="user" title="Reviewer" subtitle="Clicks an element">
    <Node id="comment" kind="document" title="Comment" subtitle="A file in .feedback/">
      <Node id="ok" title="ok" subtitle="The line is unchanged" at={1} state="success" />
      <Node id="moved" title="moved" subtitle="Found on another line" at={2} />
      <Node id="guessed" title="guessed" subtitle="The closest similar line" at={3} />
      <Node id="lost" title="lost" subtitle="Only the file is known" at={4} state="error" />
    </Node>
  </Node>
</Tree>

<Aside>

- Press `c` in the browser to comment
- Comments are committed with the deck
- Lint warns while one is open

</Aside>

<Notes>
Tomás presses c, clicks the thing he means, and types. The comment is saved as a file next to the deck, with the source line of the element he clicked.

Then I edit the slide, so the line moves. The comment has four honest answers. [click] ok: still there. [click] moved: found elsewhere. [click] guessed: reworded, here is the closest match, please check. [click] lost: I only know the file.

An agent reads the same list as JSON, with a screenshot per comment.

Transition: and the agent can also sit next to the slide.
</Notes>

slides.title: An agent turn edits a working copy, and only content reaches the deck
slides.source:

layout: diagram
title: An agent turn edits a working copy, and only content reaches the deck
eyebrow: The chat agent
surface: inverse
budget: 1m30s
---

<SequenceDiagram title="One turn of the chat agent, from the prompt to the synced slide">
  <Actor id="panel" kind="client" title="Chat panel" />
  <Actor id="host" kind="service" title="Agent host" />
  <Actor id="agent" kind="agent" title="Agent" />
  <Actor id="copy" kind="storage" title="Working copy" />
  <Actor id="deck" kind="document" title="Deck" />
  <Message from="panel" to="host" label="Prompt and slide" at={1} />
  <Message from="host" to="copy" label="Clone the content" at={2} />
  <Message from="host" to="agent" label="Run one turn" at={3} />
  <Message from="agent" to="copy" label="Edit the slide" at={4} />
  <Message from="copy" to="deck" label="Sync content only" at={5} />
  <Message from="host" to="panel" label="Lint and changes" reply at={6} />
</SequenceDiagram>

<Notes>
Here is how little the agent may do. [click] You type in the panel; the host gets the prompt and which slide you are on. [click] It clones the deck's content, slides and assets only, into a working copy. [click] It runs one turn of the agent, [click] which edits the working copy and nothing else.

[click] A sync brings changes into the deck, and it takes content files only. A config, a stylesheet, a brand file: ignored and reported. [click] Then the host lints and tells you what changed.

Every turn has an undo.

Transition: this is what it looks like from the chair.
</Notes>

Press `p` in the deck and a second window opens for the speaker.

<Aside>

### deck present

One command opens the audience window on the projector and the presenter window on the laptop.

</Aside>

<Notes>
I am reading this from the presenter window. It shows this slide, the next one, the notes, and a clock.

The clock is the useful part: the deck knows how long the talk is and every slide has a budget, so it tells me whether I am ahead or behind, per slide.

### Airlines pooled passengers at hubs

A direct flight needs enough passengers for one city pair. At a hub, passengers from many origins fill the same onward flight.

<Aside>

<Step at={1} effect="fade">

### Wrenhaul pools parcels at hubs

Nearby drops share a rider and a bike loop.

</Step>

<Step at={2} effect="fade">

### Open assumption

Can each new hub reach 250 drops a day?

</Step>

</Aside>

<Footnote>Source for the threshold: Wrenhaul’s hub model.</Footnote>

<Notes>
Pitch by analogy using `content` and two `<Step>` reveals in the aside. Start with a familiar change: airline hubs pool passengers, which makes more city pairs viable. [click] Wrenhaul pools nearby drops so one rider can make nine stops on the same loop. [click] The relevant assumption is density. If a hub cannot reach roughly 250 drops a day, pooling will not pay for the hub.
</Notes>

## Flock makes four decisions every 90 seconds

<Step at={1} focus>

- **Which drops go now:** the windows that close first

</Step>

<Step at={2} focus>

- **Which drops ride together:** neighbours, up to nine

</Step>

<Step at={3} focus>

- **In what order:** the route solver sets the stops

</Step>

<Step at={4} focus>

- **Which rider takes it:** the next one back at the hub

</Step>

<Notes>
`default` with a heading and four bullets, each in `<Step focus>`; use it when you talk through a list one point at a time and the room should look at the point you are on.
[click] First, Flock picks the drops whose windows close soonest. [click] Then it groups neighbours into a loop of up to nine. [click] The route solver orders the stops. [click] And the loop goes to the next rider back at the hub. All of it, every 90 seconds.
</Notes>

slides.title: Approve an €8M lead for expansion
slides.source:
---
layout: content
title: Approve an €8M lead for expansion
eyebrow: Saltglass investment committee
budget: 1m
---

**Thesis.** Dense hubs make same-hour delivery cheaper. Lead Wrenhaul’s €14M round to open six hubs across four new cities.

### Why invest

- **Demand is growing.** Monthly drops tripled to 182,000 in October.
- **Full loops lower cost.** The median loop carries nine drops. Cost per drop fell from €3.40 to €2.34 in a year.

<Aside>
### Reconsider if

New hubs may take too long to fill, erasing the cost advantage.

Review the expansion if either of the first two hubs averages fewer than six drops per loop at week 12.
</Aside>

<Footnote>October 2026 operating report. Saltglass’s review threshold is illustrative.</Footnote>

<Notes>
Investment committee decision using `content` with an aside. Put the commitment to a vote: €8M of the €14M round. The demand and cost evidence justify testing the thesis in more cities. The strongest objection is that the density of the existing network may not carry over. Agree to revisit expansion if either of the first two new hubs averages fewer than six drops per loop at week twelve.
</Notes>

```ts title="checkout.ts" {4-7|4-10}
import { Wrenhaul } from '@wrenhaul/sdk';

const wren = new Wrenhaul({ apiKey: process.env.WREN_KEY });
const drop = await wren.drops.create({
  pickup: 'hub:old-town',
  dropoff: '14 Weir Street',
```

```yaml title="flock.yaml" diff lineNumbers
batching:
-  interval: 300s
+  interval: 90s
  max_drops_per_loop: 9
  max_loop_minutes: 75
  overflow: partner_van
```

<Aside>
- Drops wait at most 90 seconds for a loop, not five minutes
- Hana Sato's team made the solver fast enough first
</Aside>

<Notes>

The change that made the same-hour window work was one line. Flock used to batch every five minutes; now it batches every 90 seconds, so a drop waits at most a minute and a half before it is on a loop. The line was the easy part: Hana Sato's team first had to make the solver plan a hub's loops inside that time.
</Notes>

Flock asks one question of every waiting drop: can a bike take it? Under 25 kilos, with a rider who can make the window. Then it goes on a bike loop: 93% of drops. [click] The rest: if a partner van can make the window, the van takes it, 5%; if not, we offer the recipient the next day, 2%.

slides.title: A careful first summer keeps new trees alive
slides.source:
---
layout: do-dont
title: A careful first summer keeps new trees alive
eyebrow: Watering wardens · 2027
surface: accent
labels:
  do: Help the roots establish
  dont: Avoid the common errors
reveal: true
budget: 45s
do:
  - Water slowly across the soil bed on a dry summer evening
  - Leave a clear ring around the trunk as you spread mulch
  - Check the soil below the surface before adding a bucket
  - Report damaged stakes and split ties to the arborist
dont:
  - Pour the whole bucket onto one spot beside the new trunk
  - Heap fresh mulch against the bark to hide the soil basin
  - Assume wet pavement means the soil below is damp enough
  - Tighten a loose tie until it rubs against the tree bark
---

Every watering warden follows the same guide in the first two summers after planting.

<Footnote>Larkfield watering guide, 2027; ask the duty arborist if a tree looks stressed.</Footnote>

[click] Four practical habits keep the water where a young tree needs it.

```ts title="server.ts" {3-5|4|7} lineNumbers /authenticate/
const app = createApp();

app.use(cors());
app.use(authenticate());
app.use(rateLimit({ perMinute: 60 }));

app.get('/orders', listOrders);
app.listen(3000);
```

<Aside>
- Middleware runs in the order it is registered
- `authenticate` answers 401 before any route code
- Rate limits count signed-in users, not IPs
</Aside>

<Notes>
Press next three times: first the three `use` calls, then `authenticate` on its own, then the route that depends on it.

The point for the room: order is the contract. Move `authenticate` below the route and the route is public.

If asked about the limit of 60: it is per user per minute, and the dashboard lets support raise it per account.
</Notes>

```ts title="orders.ts" diff lineNumbers /requireUser/
  return db.orders.where({ userId: user.id });
}
```

<Aside>
- `requireUser` throws `Unauthorized`, which the error handler turns into a 401
- One line per route, no new branches
</Aside>

<Notes>
Read the two changed lines aloud. Before, `req.user` was undefined for expired sessions and `user.id` threw a TypeError, which surfaced as a 500.

The marked word is the whole change.
</Notes>

slides.source:
---
layout: diagram
title: Every checkout crosses five hops before the first byte comes back
eyebrow: The request path
budget: 2m
---

<Flow title="A checkout request's path through the Parcelwise web stack">
  <Node id="browser" kind="client" title="Browser" subtitle="React app" col={1} row={1} />
  <Node id="cdn" kind="cloud" title="Edge CDN" subtitle="120 PoPs" col={2} row={1} />
  <Group label="Production VPC">
    <Node id="gateway" kind="gateway" title="API gateway" subtitle="Auth" col={3} row={1} />
    <Node id="orders" kind="service" title="Orders service" subtitle="6 pods" col={4} row={1} />
    <Node id="cache" kind="cache" title="Session cache" subtitle="Redis" col={3} row={2} />
    <Node id="db" kind="database" title="Orders DB" subtitle="Postgres 16" col={5} row={1} />
    <Node id="queue" kind="queue" title="Order events" subtitle="Kafka" col={5} row={2} />
  </Group>
  <Edge from="browser" to="cdn" label="HTTPS" />
  <Edge from="cdn" to="gateway" />
  <Edge from="gateway" to="orders" label="gRPC" />
  <Edge from="orders" to="cache" label="Session" />
  <Edge from="orders" to="db" label="SQL" />
  <Edge from="orders" to="queue" label="Events" async />
  <Journey at={1} path="browser cdn gateway orders db" back focus />
</Flow>

<Notes>
Walk the request one hop per click. The browser hits the CDN, which forwards the API call to the gateway; the gateway authenticates and hands it to the orders service, which reads the order from Postgres. Then the response comes back the same way.

The cache and the event stream dim while the request travels: they are not on this path.
</Notes>

title: One order event fans out to three teams without a single direct call
eyebrow: Event-driven
budget: 1m30s
---

<Flow title="Order events fanning out from the orders service to three consumers">
  <Node id="orders" kind="service" title="Orders service" col={1} row={2} />
  <Node id="bus" kind="queue" title="order.placed" subtitle="Kafka topic, 12 partitions" col={2} row={2} />
  <Node id="billing" kind="function" title="Billing" subtitle="Invoices" col={3} row={1} />
  <Node id="shipping" kind="service" title="Shipping" subtitle="Labels and pickup" col={3} row={2} />
  <Node id="notify" kind="function" title="Notifications" subtitle="Email and SMS" col={3} row={3} />
  <Edge from="orders" to="bus" label="publish" flow={{ count: 3 }} />
  <Edge from="bus" to="billing" async at={1} />
  <Edge from="bus" to="shipping" async at={1} />
  <Edge from="bus" to="notify" async at={1} />
  <Packet path="bus billing" at={2} until={4} count={2} />
  <Packet path="bus shipping" at={2} until={4} count={2} />
  <Packet path="bus notify" at={2} until={4} count={2} />
  <State node="notify" at={3} is="success" badge="Sent" />
</Flow>

<Aside>
### No coupling

Orders publishes once and moves on. Each consumer reads at its own pace and can be down without blocking checkout.
</Aside>

<Notes>
Start with the steady stream into the topic: that is every order, all day. Click once to show the three subscribers, again to send the event to all three at the same time.

The point is the arrows that are missing: orders never calls billing, shipping or notifications directly.
</Notes>

layout: diagram
title: The support agent answers in one loop of think, call, observe
eyebrow: AI agent
surface: inverse
budget: 2m
---

<Flow title="The support agent's loop between the customer, the model and three tools">
  <Node id="customer" kind="user" title="Customer" subtitle="Where is my parcel?" col={1} row={2} />
  <Node id="agent" kind="agent" title="Support agent" subtitle="Plans each turn" col={2} row={2} />
  <Node id="model" kind="llm" title="Language model" col={2} row={1} />
  <Group label="Tools">
    <Node id="tracking" kind="tool" title="Track parcel" col={3} row={1} />
    <Node id="orders" kind="tool" title="Look up order" col={3} row={2} />
    <Node id="kb" kind="document" title="Help articles" col={3} row={3} />
  </Group>
  <Edge from="customer" to="agent" bidirectional />
  <Edge from="agent" to="model" bidirectional />
  <Edge from="agent" to="tracking" />
  <Edge from="agent" to="orders" />
  <Edge from="agent" to="kb" />
  <Journey at={1}>
    <Hop from="customer" to="agent" label="Question" />
    <Hop from="agent" to="model" label="Plan" reply="Call: lookup" />
    <Hop from="agent" to="orders" label="PW-48213" reply="Shipped" />
    <Hop from="agent" to="tracking" label="Tracking" reply="Out for delivery" />
    <Hop from="agent" to="customer" label="Answer" returning />
  </Journey>
</Flow>

<Notes>
Five clicks, five moves. The question arrives; the agent asks the model what to do; the model says look up the order; the agent calls the order tool, then the tracking tool, each answer coming back as a ring; then it answers the customer.

Every call goes through the agent: the model never touches a tool directly. That is the property that lets us log and limit every action.
</Notes>

title: A slow card network no longer takes checkout down

surface: accent
budget: 2m
---

<Flow title="A card payment that times out, is queued and retried, then succeeds">
  <Node id="checkout" kind="service" title="Checkout" col={1} row={1} />
  <Node id="payments" kind="service" title="Payments" subtitle="Circuit breaker" col={2} row={1} />
  <Node id="network" kind="external" title="Card network" col={3} row={1} />
  <Node id="retries" kind="queue" title="Retry queue" subtitle="Backoff 2, 4, 8 s" col={2} row={2} />
  <Edge from="checkout" to="payments" label="Charge" />
  <Edge from="payments" to="network" label="Authorize" />
  <Edge from="payments" to="retries" label="Park" at={2} async />
  <Packet path="checkout payments network" at={1} label="€42.10" />
  <State node="network" at={2} until={4} is="error" badge="Timeout" />
  <State edge="payments->network" at={2} until={4} is="error" />
  <Packet path="payments retries" at={2} />
  <State node="checkout" at={2} until={4} is="success" badge="Order held" />
  <Packet path="retries payments network" at={3} label="Retry 2" play="once" />
  <State node="network" at={4} is="success" badge="Approved" />
  <Packet from="payments" to="network" at={4} reply="Approved" />
</Flow>

<Aside>
### Before

A timeout here used to fail the whole checkout. Now the order is held and the charge retried in the background.
</Aside>

<Notes>
Step one is the happy path. Step two is the bad afternoon: the card network times out, the circuit breaker parks the charge, and checkout tells the customer the order is held. Step three is the retry with backoff; step four the approval.
</Notes>

slides.title: Shade is infrastructure
slides.source: --- layout: title title: Shade is infrastructure eyebrow: Budget committee briefing byline: Dana Okafor, Urban Forestry Division date: 18 November 2026 surface: default budget: 45s --- import street from '../assets/westgate-street.jpg'; A ten-year canopy plan for the neighbourhoods that heat up first. Thank the chair. Say what you want by the end: approval of the ten-year canopy line in the 2027 capital plan. Do not explain the photo yet. It comes back on slide ten.

slides.title: The hottest afternoon of 2026
slides.source:
---
layout: statement
title: The hottest afternoon of 2026
eyebrow: 12 July 2026, 3 p.m.
budget: 40s
---

An Eastgate bus stop hit 51 °C. Under Riverside's oaks it was 38 °C.

<Notes>
Let the numbers sit. Pause for a full breath before you go on.

Riverside is four kilometres west of the bus stop.

Both readings are from the same survey flight, ten minutes apart. The difference is not the weather; it is the street.
</Notes>

slides.title: Why Eastgate
slides.source:
---
layout: section
title: Why Eastgate
number: 1
eyebrow: Part one
budget: 15s
---

The district with the least shade has the most people at risk from heat.

<Notes>
Three slides of evidence, then one voice from the hospital.
</Notes>

slides.title: Eastgate has a quarter of Riverside's shade
slides.source:
---
layout: stats
title: Eastgate has a quarter of Riverside's shade
eyebrow: Canopy cover
stats:
  - value: 9%
    label: of Eastgate's ground under tree crowns at noon
    delta: −3 pts since 2016
  - value: 34%
    label: of Riverside's ground under tree crowns at noon
    delta: +1 pt since 2016
budget: 1m
---

The gap has widened for ten years: Eastgate loses more trees to storms and roadworks than it plants.

<Footnote>Source: Larkfield summer aerial survey, 2016 and 2026.</Footnote>

<Notes>
The city average is 21%. Eastgate is the lowest of our fourteen districts.

If asked about the losses: 410 trees removed since 2016, 160 replanted.
</Notes>

slides.title: The heat follows the missing trees
slides.source: --- layout: split title: The heat follows the missing trees eyebrow: Surface temperature ratio: 5:7 treatment: plain budget: 1m30s --- import heatMap from '../assets/eastgate-heat-map.jpg'; Block by block, the hottest ground is where the canopy is thinnest. - The five hottest blocks all have under 5% cover - Riverside's parks ran 12 °C cooler than nearby streets Land surface temperature, 12 July 2026, 3 p.m. Survey flight on a 30 m grid. Point at the river first, then follow the colour east into Eastgate. The one cool patch inside Eastgate is the Holloway Road pilot. We come back to it in part two.

slides.title: Why the heat lands hardest in Eastgate
slides.source:
---
layout: content
title: Why the heat lands hardest in Eastgate
eyebrow: The problem
budget: 1m30s
---

- Canopy cover is 9%, the lowest of our fourteen districts
- 71% of the ground is roof, road or car park
- Two in three homes are flats with no cross-ventilation
- One resident in five is over 65 or under 5
- Night-time lows stayed above 24 °C for nine nights in July
- Fewer than half of households have air conditioning

<Footnote>Sources: 2026 aerial survey, 2025 census, Larkfield housing register.</Footnote>

<Notes>
These six facts compound. Hot ground, homes that cannot cool, and people who cannot cope with heat, all on the same twelve blocks.

The night-time figure is the one the hospital cares about most. Bodies recover at night; in Eastgate they cannot.
</Notes>

slides.title: What the night nurses told us
slides.source:
---
layout: statement
title: What the night nurses told us
eyebrow: From the ward
surface: gradient
budget: 30s
---

The worst nights are the second and third of a heatwave, when the flats never cool down and our older patients stop sleeping.

<Attribution>Mariam Haddad, charge nurse, Eastgate General Hospital</Attribution>

<Notes>
Mariam gave us permission to quote her. She has worked nights at Eastgate General for eleven years.

Read the quote slowly, then move on without comment.
</Notes>

slides.title: What the pilot showed
slides.source:
---
layout: section
title: What the pilot showed
number: 2
eyebrow: Part two
budget: 10s
---

<Notes>
Three summers, 38 blocks, one question: does planting bring the temperature down fast enough to matter?
</Notes>

<Notes>

Survival is the number that surprised us. Aftercare is in the budget for that reason.
</Notes>

slides.title: A street tree is a cooling system
slides.source: --- layout: split title: A street tree is a cooling system eyebrow: How shade works side: left bleed: true budget: 1m --- import street from '../assets/westgate-street.jpg'; A mature maple shades 90 m² of pavement and evaporates up to 400 litres a day. - Shaded asphalt runs up to 20 °C cooler - The effect peaks after 15 to 20 years Westgate, July. Photo: Onthehilltop, CC0. This is the street from the cover. Ask the room to look at where the shadow falls: on the pavement and the front of the house, at three in the afternoon. The 400 litres is a peak figure for a large tree on a dry day; the usual summer figure is about half.

slides.title: Big species, not more saplings
slides.source: --- layout: split title: Big species, not more saplings eyebrow: Design choice ratio: 7:5 surface: inverse budget: 1m30s --- import square from '../assets/frederiksplein-trees.jpg'; Small ornamental trees are cheaper to plant, but most of the cooling comes from the largest crowns. - A plane tree at 20 years shades eight times the ground of a flowering pear - Large species need 12 m³ of soil, so we build connected pits under the pavement Two trees shade a whole square in Amsterdam. Photo: Fons Heijnsbroek, CC0. Small species stay on streets under 9 m wide, where a large crown would reach the buildings. This is the slide engineers will push back on. The soil volume is the reason big trees survive; without it they stall at ten years. Each connected pit costs $2,900 more than a standard one and pays for itself by year 14, from avoided pavement repairs and cooling costs alone, not health savings.

slides.title: What we are asking the committee to approve
slides.source:
---
layout: content
title: What we are asking the committee to approve
eyebrow: The ask
budget: 1m30s
---

A ten-year capital line, reviewed every three years against the canopy target.

- $4.2M a year from 2027 to 2036, $42M in total
- 6,000 large-species trees, 4,800 of them in Eastgate and Millbrook
- Three arborist posts to run planting and aftercare

<Aside>

### The target

Raise Eastgate's canopy cover from 9% to 25% by 2040, the level at which July afternoons stay below the hospital's heat-alert threshold.

</Aside>

<Notes>
The three-yearly review is the safeguard. If the pilot numbers do not hold, the committee can stop the line.

Millbrook is the second-hottest district; it gets the remaining trees from 2030.
</Notes>
